questions.topic: Review of an adverse preliminary license-transfer evaluation
questions.trigger: NABP tells a pharmacist seeking Massachusetts licensure by reciprocity that the applicant does not meet the transfer requirements. The applicant believes that NABP misunderstood an official licensing record. What is the appropriate next step under the Massachusetts reciprocity regulation?
questions.legal_decision: Submit a written request asking the Massachusetts Board to review the basis of NABP's decision.
questions.critical_exception: NABP has issued a negative preliminary evaluation; no Massachusetts license has been issued.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If NABP instead approves the preliminary application, the adverse-evaluation review procedure is unnecessary; ordinary Board approval still remains.
questions.stem: NABP tells a pharmacist seeking Massachusetts licensure by reciprocity that the applicant does not meet the transfer requirements. The applicant believes that NABP misunderstood an official licensing record. What is the appropriate next step under the Massachusetts reciprocity regulation?

choices.text: Request a final decision from the pharmacy's prospective employer.
choices.why: Incorrect. An employer cannot review eligibility for Massachusetts reciprocity.

choices.text: Begin practice on the other state's license while challenging the evaluation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Out-of-state licensure alone does not authorize Massachusetts practice.

choices.text: Ask the Massachusetts Board in writing to review the basis of NABP's decision.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation provides this specific review pathway and preserves the Board's final authority.

choices.text: Require NABP to issue the Massachusetts license directly after reviewing the record.
choices.why: Incorrect. NABP acts as the Board's preliminary evaluation agent, not the licensing authority.

choices.text: Use the reciprocity denial as a waiver of all state examination requirements.
choices.why: Incorrect. A negative preliminary evaluation does not waive the Massachusetts licensing requirements.

questions.topic: Investigative conference before a formal disciplinary proceeding
questions.trigger: A pharmacist receives a Board letter about a complaint. No formal adjudicatory proceeding has commenced. The investigator proposes a conference to discuss the issues and possible resolution. Which statements accurately describe this stage?
questions.legal_decision: Recognize that a pre-hearing investigative conference is discretionary; require timely notice with a general statement of the issues.
questions.critical_exception: The conference precedes formal adjudication; it is not itself a final disciplinary order.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If formal adjudication has already commenced, the particular pre-commencement authority in 10.04 is no longer the stated basis for scheduling the conference.
questions.stem: A pharmacist receives a Board letter about a complaint. No formal adjudicatory proceeding has commenced. The investigator proposes a conference to discuss the issues and possible resolution. Which statements accurately describe this stage? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The Board must first enter a final suspension before scheduling the conference.
choices.why: Incorrect. The purpose is to facilitate disposition before a formal proceeding begins.

choices.text: The Board may schedule a conference before formal adjudication starts.
choices.why: Correct. This is a discretionary step specifically authorized by 10.04.

choices.text: The pharmacist has automatically been formally reprimanded by receiving the letter.
choices.why: Incorrect. A notice of an investigative conference is not a final formal disciplinary action.

choices.text: The Board must hold a conference in every case before deciding to schedule a hearing.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation allows a conference or a formal hearing as appropriate.

choices.text: The notice must be timely and generally describe the nature of the issues.
choices.why: Correct. Section 10.04 expressly specifies these notice requirements.

questions.topic: Written voluntary surrender of a pharmacist registration
questions.trigger: A pharmacist negotiates a voluntary surrender of a Massachusetts personal registration for a fixed period as part of a Board consent agreement. The pharmacist proposes an oral promise to stop working, with automatic restoration when the period ends. Which provisions are required for the voluntary surrender agreement?
questions.legal_decision: Require a signed written agreement, facts and reinstatement terms, and acknowledgement of loss of registration privileges and no judicial review.
questions.critical_exception: The parties choose a voluntary surrender under 247 CMR 10.06(6), not a unilateral emergency suspension.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the Board instead issues a contested final order after adjudication, the specific voluntary-surrender agreement provisions are not the governing procedure.
questions.stem: A pharmacist negotiates a voluntary surrender of a Massachusetts personal registration for a fixed period as part of a Board consent agreement. The pharmacist proposes an oral promise to stop working, with automatic restoration when the period ends. Which provisions are required for the voluntary surrender agreement? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The pharmacist and the Board sign the written surrender agreement.
choices.why: Correct. A written document signed by both parties is required.

choices.text: A verbal undertaking to stop working satisfies the surrender procedure.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation requires a written agreement.

choices.text: The agreement recites the underlying facts and addresses reinstatement and applicable conditions.
choices.why: Correct. The agreement must include those provisions; expiration alone does not establish unrestricted reinstatement.

choices.text: The agreement acknowledges the loss of all registration privileges and the absence of judicial review of the voluntary surrender.
choices.why: Correct. These acknowledgements are required by the specific voluntary-surrender provision.

choices.text: The Board must remove the agreement from its permanent records immediately upon reinstatement.
choices.why: Incorrect. The agreement becomes part of the permanent Board records.

questions.topic: Attempt to compromise a licensing examination
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy intern is caught attempting to obtain and distribute secure licensing examination content before the test. The intern argues that no prescription was dispensed incorrectly and the attempted compromise failed. What is the Board's authority under its disciplinary regulation?
questions.legal_decision: Treat attempting to compromise exam integrity as an independent possible ground for discipline.
questions.critical_exception: The individual already holds a Board-issued intern license; actual patient injury is not a condition of this ground.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the intern merely studies lawfully released public sample items without attempting to compromise the exam, this ground is not established by those facts.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy intern is caught attempting to obtain and distribute secure licensing examination content before the test. The intern argues that no prescription was dispensed incorrectly and the attempted compromise failed. What is the Board's authority under its disciplinary regulation?

choices.text: The Board may act only if the intern actually obtains a passing examination score.
choices.why: Incorrect. An attempt to compromise exam integrity is itself listed.

choices.text: The Board must wait until a patient is harmed by an incorrect dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient harm is not an element of the examination-integrity ground.

choices.text: The matter is exclusively an academic issue outside the Board's disciplinary authority.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board's regulation expressly covers licensing examination misconduct.

choices.text: The attempt may independently support disciplinary action against the intern.
choices.why: Correct. Section 10.03(1)(s) covers cheating and attempted compromise.

choices.text: The attempt requires the Board to issue an automatic permanent revocation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The provision supplies a ground for discipline, not an automatic mandatory sanction.

questions.topic: CDTM qualification: relevant portion of current practice
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacist meets the licensure, experience, insurance and continuing-education requirements for a proposed CDTM agreement concerning diabetes. The pharmacist plans to perform exclusively unrelated administrative duties and devote no portion of current pharmacy practice to the defined diabetes therapy area. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.legal_decision: Require the pharmacist to devote a portion of practice to the drug therapy area that will be co-managed.
questions.critical_exception: The pharmacist seeks to qualify for CDTM; no minimum percentage is specified by this clause.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist devotes a portion of actual practice to the defined therapy area and meets the other criteria, this qualification defect is resolved.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist meets the licensure, experience, insurance and continuing-education requirements for a proposed CDTM agreement concerning diabetes. The pharmacist plans to perform exclusively unrelated administrative duties and devote no portion of current pharmacy practice to the defined diabetes therapy area. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: Arrange for the pharmacist to devote a portion of practice to the defined diabetes therapy area.
choices.why: Correct. This is an independent CDTM qualification in 16.02(1)(d).

choices.text: Accept any administrative role because five years of experience replaces the other qualifications.
choices.why: Incorrect. The years of experience do not replace the defined-area practice requirement.

choices.text: Require the pharmacist to devote every working hour exclusively to diabetes management.
choices.why: Incorrect. The clause requires a portion of practice, not exclusive practice.

choices.text: Allow the supervising physician's experience to satisfy this pharmacist-specific condition.
choices.why: Incorrect. The obligation applies to the participating pharmacist.

choices.text: Require the pharmacist to obtain a new PharmD degree before addressing the practice allocation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The stated defect is practice in the defined area, not the pharmacist's existing degree.

questions.topic: CDTM evidence of continuing education after agreement date
questions.trigger: An authorized pharmacist begins a new two-year CDTM agreement. After completing the first year's additional CDTM education, the pharmacist proposes deleting its documentation when that year ends. What minimum retention period applies under the CDTM-specific rule, independently of other record-retention requirements?
questions.legal_decision: Keep evidence of required CDTM CE for at least two years after the date of the current agreement.
questions.critical_exception: The CDTM evidence rule applies independently of general pharmacist CE record obligations.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If two years have elapsed after the current agreement date, this particular minimum is met, but another applicable retention requirement may still prevent deletion.
questions.stem: An authorized pharmacist begins a new two-year CDTM agreement. After completing the first year's additional CDTM education, the pharmacist proposes deleting its documentation when that year ends. What minimum retention period applies under the CDTM-specific rule, independently of other record-retention requirements?

choices.text: Keep the evidence until the next CDTM continuing education course is completed.
choices.why: Incorrect. Completing another course does not end the required retention period.

choices.text: Keep the evidence for at least two years after the date of the current agreement.
choices.why: Correct. Section 16.02(2) establishes this agreement-based minimum.

choices.text: Keep the evidence only until the supervising physician acknowledges its completion.
choices.why: Incorrect. Physician acknowledgment does not replace the pharmacist's retention duty.

choices.text: Keep the evidence through the end of the first agreement year, then delete it.
choices.why: Incorrect. The first year alone does not satisfy the two-year minimum.

choices.text: Keep the evidence only if the pharmacist prescribes Schedule II controlled substances.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule applies to participating authorized pharmacists.

questions.topic: Community CDTM: employment of a supervising physician
questions.trigger: A community pharmacy plans to employ a physician for two separate purposes: reviewing pharmacists' CDTM quality assurance and serving as the physician hired specifically to establish the pharmacy's CDTM agreements. Which arrangement is permitted under Massachusetts CDTM rules?
questions.legal_decision: Permit employment for quality assurance reviews but not employment of a physician for establishing or maintaining CDTM agreements.
questions.critical_exception: The setting is a community pharmacy, and the purpose of employment is decisive.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the physician employs a qualified pharmacist to provide CDTM for the physician's own patients under an agreement, the regulation permits that employment relationship.
questions.stem: A community pharmacy plans to employ a physician for two separate purposes: reviewing pharmacists' CDTM quality assurance and serving as the physician hired specifically to establish the pharmacy's CDTM agreements. Which arrangement is permitted under Massachusetts CDTM rules?

choices.text: Hire a physician for both purposes because the physician is licensed in Massachusetts.
choices.why: Incorrect. Licensure does not remove the express employment restriction.

choices.text: Hire a qualified clinician for quality assurance, but not a physician to establish the agreements.
choices.why: Correct. The community pharmacy may hire a physician or licensed practitioner for quality assurance; the second purpose is prohibited.

choices.text: Prohibit a physician group from hiring qualified pharmacists to provide CDTM to its patients.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation expressly permits that physician-to-pharmacist employment arrangement.

choices.text: Permit the second arrangement if the pharmacy pays a salary rather than a referral fee.
choices.why: Incorrect. The purpose of the employment, not its compensation format, controls.

choices.text: Treat quality assurance employment as automatic approval of all CDTM prescribing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Quality assurance review does not substitute for a compliant collaborative agreement.

questions.topic: Ambulatory clinic CDTM: absent attending physician
questions.trigger: A licensed Massachusetts ambulatory care clinic plans to begin CDTM under a signed current collaborative practice agreement. The clinic has not obtained the required institutional approval, and its affiliated attending physician will be off site, available only by phone. Which clinic-specific conditions must be satisfied before beginning?
questions.legal_decision: Arrange the required on-site supervision and obtain the appropriate clinic committee or medical-director approval.
questions.critical_exception: Ambulatory care clinic, not a community pharmacy; no overriding authorization or waiver is assumed.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If both the on-site supervision and appropriate institutional approval are in place, these two specific practice-setting defects are resolved.
questions.stem: A licensed Massachusetts ambulatory care clinic plans to begin CDTM under a signed current collaborative practice agreement. The clinic has not obtained the required institutional approval, and its affiliated attending physician will be off site, available only by phone. Which clinic-specific conditions must be satisfied before beginning? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Arrange on-site supervision by an affiliated attending physician and an authorized pharmacist.
choices.why: Correct. Section 16.03(4) requires the specified on-site supervision.

choices.text: Rely on the signed agreement alone as a substitute for institutional approval.
choices.why: Incorrect. The current agreement does not replace the clinic-specific approval.

choices.text: Substitute telephone-only physician availability for the required on-site supervision.
choices.why: Incorrect. The clinic's setting-specific rule expressly calls for on-site supervision.

choices.text: Obtain approval from the clinic medical staff executive committee or medical director, or a designee.
choices.why: Correct. Section 16.03(4) permits these approval pathways.

choices.text: Use the community pharmacy practice-setting rule because the patients receive outpatient care.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation distinguishes ambulatory clinics from retail pharmacies.

questions.topic: CDTM delegation: agreement silent on nondelegable duties
questions.trigger: A hospital pharmacist participating in CDTM asks an experienced technician to assume a patient-support task. The collaborative agreement says only that staff may assist as needed; it does not specify what duties may be delegated, when delegation occurs, or its duration. Which changes are required before relying on delegation under the agreement?
questions.legal_decision: Specify delegable and nondelegable duties, delegation conditions/duration/scope, and preserve each worker's independent legal scope.
questions.critical_exception: A collaborative agreement is required to specify delegation parameters even if the proposed worker is otherwise appropriately trained.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the agreement specifies the duty and delegation conditions and the worker has legal authority, this agreement-based barrier is removed.
questions.stem: A hospital pharmacist participating in CDTM asks an experienced technician to assume a patient-support task. The collaborative agreement says only that staff may assist as needed; it does not specify what duties may be delegated, when delegation occurs, or its duration. Which changes are required before relying on delegation under the agreement? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Identify which agreement duties may and may not be delegated.
choices.why: Correct. The agreement must distinguish delegable from nondelegable duties.

choices.text: Use the technician's experience to replace the written delegation terms.
choices.why: Incorrect. Experience does not remove the agreement-content requirement.

choices.text: Specify when and how delegation occurs and its duration and scope.
choices.why: Correct. Section 16.04(3) requires those parameters.

choices.text: Authorize the technician to exercise any pharmacist clinical judgment named in the agreement.
choices.why: Incorrect. The agreement cannot expand a technician beyond the legally authorized scope.

choices.text: Ensure intern and technician tasks also comply with their respective professional regulations.
choices.why: Correct. The CDTM provision expressly cross-references the personnel rules.

questions.topic: HIPAA disclosure to a deceased patient's former caregiver
questions.trigger: A patient died six months ago. The patient's adult daughter collected medications and paid for them during the patient's life. She is not the estate's personal representative and now asks for every prescription record, including unrelated confidential therapies. No contrary preference expressed by the patient is known. Under HIPAA alone, what may the pharmacy disclose?
questions.legal_decision: Disclose information relevant to the daughter's prior involvement in care or payment, not the entire unrelated record merely because of family relationship.
questions.critical_exception: The patient died less than 50 years ago; the daughter was involved in care/payment and no known contrary preference applies.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the daughter establishes authority as the decedent's personal representative, her rights are evaluated under that distinct provision.
questions.stem: A patient died six months ago. The patient's adult daughter collected medications and paid for them during the patient's life. She is not the estate's personal representative and now asks for every prescription record, including unrelated confidential therapies. No contrary preference expressed by the patient is known. Under HIPAA alone, what may the pharmacy disclose?

choices.text: Release the complete record because HIPAA protection ends at death.
choices.why: Incorrect. Identifiable health information remains protected for 50 years after death.

choices.text: Decline every disclosure unless the daughter is appointed executor.
choices.why: Incorrect. The caregiver/payment-involvement provision allows limited disclosure without personal-representative status.

choices.text: Provide unrelated confidential therapies because the requester is an adult child.
choices.why: Incorrect. Family relationship does not remove the relevance and prior-preference limits.

choices.text: Treat a death certificate as written authorization for disclosure of every therapy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Proof of death is not a general authorization for complete disclosure.

choices.text: Disclose relevant information about the care or payment in which the daughter was involved.
choices.why: Correct. The limited disclosure is permissible under the stated conditions.

questions.topic: Research treatment records: temporary HIPAA access suspension
questions.trigger: A covered health care provider participates in a treatment research study. At enrollment the patient agreed to temporary suspension of access to PHI created during that study and was told access would be restored when the study ended. The study remains in progress. Which statements describe the HIPAA access rule for those records?
questions.legal_decision: Permit a temporary access denial for the study records during the research under the documented consent conditions; restore the right when research ends.
questions.critical_exception: This is treatment research and the two specific consent/information conditions are satisfied; the suspension is not for unrelated routine records.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the patient did not agree to temporary denial at enrollment, the stated research exception would not support denial.
questions.stem: A covered health care provider participates in a treatment research study. At enrollment the patient agreed to temporary suspension of access to PHI created during that study and was told access would be restored when the study ended. The study remains in progress. Which statements describe the HIPAA access rule for those records? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Withhold all pharmacy records indefinitely because the patient entered research.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception is temporary and limited to the relevant research PHI.

choices.text: Temporarily deny access to the covered study records while the research remains in progress.
choices.why: Correct. The stated research and consent conditions satisfy this access exception.

choices.text: Reinstate the right of access after the research is completed.
choices.why: Correct. The patient must have been informed of reinstatement and the exception lasts only during research.

choices.text: Use the exception even if the patient's participation consent never mentioned denial of access.
choices.why: Incorrect. Agreement to the denial as part of consent is an express condition.

choices.text: Extend the suspension for five additional years solely to simplify record archiving.
choices.why: Incorrect. The research exception does not authorize a post-study archival delay.

questions.topic: HIPAA product-safety disclosure to FDA-regulated manufacturer
questions.trigger: A pharmacist discovers a serious suspected defect in a specific FDA-regulated drug. The manufacturer responsible for that product requests limited patient information necessary to investigate the product problem and contact affected users for a recall. Assume ordinary HIPAA records, no special confidentiality law, and appropriate minimum-necessary safeguards. Which conclusions are correct?
questions.legal_decision: Permit a limited PHI disclosure to the responsible FDA-regulated person for authorized product safety and recall purposes without individual authorization.
questions.critical_exception: The recipient is responsible for the FDA-regulated product and the use is within the specified product-safety purposes.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the same request were instead for unrelated commercial advertising, the product-safety exception would not authorize that disclosure.
questions.stem: A pharmacist discovers a serious suspected defect in a specific FDA-regulated drug. The manufacturer responsible for that product requests limited patient information necessary to investigate the product problem and contact affected users for a recall. Assume ordinary HIPAA records, no special confidentiality law, and appropriate minimum-necessary safeguards. Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Disclose the necessary relevant information for investigation of the product defect.
choices.why: Correct. The public-health provision covers responsible FDA-regulated persons investigating product defects.

choices.text: Disclose complete unrelated prescription histories for future promotional campaigns.
choices.why: Incorrect. The permitted product-safety purpose does not authorize unrelated marketing.

choices.text: Require individual authorization solely because the recipient is a private manufacturer.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception expressly includes a responsible person subject to FDA jurisdiction.

choices.text: Disclose relevant information for locating and notifying patients affected by the recall.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation identifies product recall and lookback activities as permitted purposes.

choices.text: Treat the disclosure permission as a requirement to send every patient's entire pharmacy record.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception is not an unrestricted disclosure mandate.

questions.topic: Known material breach of business associate agreement
questions.trigger: A pharmacy learns that its contracted claims vendor repeatedly uses PHI outside the purposes permitted by the business associate agreement. The vendor continues the material violation despite the pharmacy's initial objections. Which steps address the covered entity's obligations under the HIPAA organizational requirements?
questions.legal_decision: Take reasonable steps to cure the breach or end the violation; if unsuccessful, terminate the arrangement if feasible.
questions.critical_exception: The covered entity knows of a pattern of material violations of the business associate's contractual obligations.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If reasonable corrective steps successfully end the violation, the specified termination-if-feasible step is not triggered by unsuccessful remediation.
questions.stem: A pharmacy learns that its contracted claims vendor repeatedly uses PHI outside the purposes permitted by the business associate agreement. The vendor continues the material violation despite the pharmacy's initial objections. Which steps address the covered entity's obligations under the HIPAA organizational requirements? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Ignore the violation because the vendor signed a business associate agreement.
choices.why: Incorrect. A signed agreement does not excuse the covered entity's knowledge of a material violation.

choices.text: Wait for proof of patient financial harm before taking contractual corrective action.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation does not make financial harm a prerequisite.

choices.text: Take reasonable steps to cure the breach or end the violation.
choices.why: Correct. This is the required response to the known material pattern.

choices.text: Allow the vendor to continue the prohibited use merely because it processes claims.
choices.why: Incorrect. A legitimate claims function does not justify conduct outside the agreement.

choices.text: If those steps are unsuccessful, terminate the arrangement if feasible.
choices.why: Correct. This is the specified next step after failed remediation.

questions.topic: Patient revocation of a HIPAA authorization
questions.trigger: A patient signed a valid authorization permitting the pharmacy to disclose a defined set of records to a third party. The pharmacy already made one authorized disclosure yesterday. Today the pharmacy receives the patient's written revocation before a scheduled second disclosure. No other legal basis for the second disclosure applies. What should the pharmacy do?
questions.legal_decision: Stop the planned disclosure that would rely solely on the revoked authorization; recognize that the prior reliance-based disclosure is not retroactively invalidated.
questions.critical_exception: The covered entity has received the written revocation, and the second disclosure has not occurred.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the authorization remains valid and has not been revoked or expired, a disclosure within its scope may proceed.
questions.stem: A patient signed a valid authorization permitting the pharmacy to disclose a defined set of records to a third party. The pharmacy already made one authorized disclosure yesterday. Today the pharmacy receives the patient's written revocation before a scheduled second disclosure. No other legal basis for the second disclosure applies. What should the pharmacy do?

choices.text: Stop the planned second disclosure; the earlier lawful reliance is not undone.
choices.why: Correct. A written revocation is effective on receipt except to the extent of action already taken in reliance.

choices.text: Continue all planned disclosures through the original expiration date.
choices.why: Incorrect. Revocation can end permission before the expiration date.

choices.text: Automatically classify the earlier disclosure as an unlawful breach solely because of the later revocation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The reliance exception protects actions already taken under the valid authorization.

choices.text: Require the third party to approve the patient's decision before honoring it.
choices.why: Incorrect. Revocation is the patient's right, not the recipient's veto.

choices.text: Stop providing routine pharmacy treatment because a separate authorization was revoked.
choices.why: Incorrect. The revocation does not eliminate ordinary permitted treatment activities.

questions.topic: Hospital narcotic maintenance incidental to treatment of another condition
questions.trigger: A patient with opioid dependence is admitted for treatment of a serious unrelated infection. The hospital's authorized physician orders administration of a narcotic during the hospitalization to prevent withdrawal as an incidental adjunct to treatment of that infection. The hospital is otherwise authorized to possess and administer the drug. Under the federal narcotic-treatment rule, which conclusion is correct?
questions.legal_decision: Recognize the hospital incidental-adjunct exception without converting it into routine outpatient maintenance prescribing authority.
questions.critical_exception: The narcotic administration occurs in the hospital and is incidental to medical treatment of a condition other than addiction.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If instead the practitioner wants to routinely dispense Schedule II narcotics solely for maintenance treatment outside the incidental hospital context, separate narcotic treatment program requirements or another applicable exception must be met.
questions.stem: A patient with opioid dependence is admitted for treatment of a serious unrelated infection. The hospital's authorized physician orders administration of a narcotic during the hospitalization to prevent withdrawal as an incidental adjunct to treatment of that infection. The hospital is otherwise authorized to possess and administer the drug. Under the federal narcotic-treatment rule, which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: The physician must limit this inpatient administration to the same three-day referral supply in every case.
choices.why: Incorrect. The incidental hospital treatment provision is distinct from the emergency referral rule.

choices.text: The order automatically authorizes an ordinary outpatient maintenance prescription after discharge.
choices.why: Incorrect. The hospital exception does not confer unrestricted outpatient maintenance prescribing authority.

choices.text: The hospital must register as an opioid treatment program solely because this incidental inpatient care occurs.
choices.why: Incorrect. Subsection (c) expressly preserves this incidental hospital administration authority.

choices.text: The hospital may administer under the incidental-adjunct provision, assuming other laws are met.
choices.why: Correct. The specified treatment of an unrelated infection fits the federal exception.

choices.text: The exemption permits the hospital to ignore all controlled-substance records.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception does not waive applicable registration, security or recordkeeping duties.

questions.topic: Pharmacist administration: prescriber reassessment and intent notation
questions.trigger: An adult presents a valid prescription with refills for an eligible long-acting injectable antipsychotic in single-dose packaging. The prescription lacks the suggested 'for pharmacist administration' notation. The trained pharmacist believes the prescriber intends pharmacy administration and has questions about the time since the last prescriber reassessment. Assume all other legal and clinical prerequisites are met. Which statements reflect DPH Circular DCP 26-03-124?
questions.legal_decision: Treat the intent notation as encouraged rather than mandatory; clarify intended administration and reassessment timing as appropriate; recognize that valid refills can coexist with prescriber-determined reassessment intervals.
questions.critical_exception: The prescription is otherwise valid; the circular encourages clarification of intended administration and reassessment timing rather than making these communications mandatory in every case.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a valid prescription is absent or a clinical or legal prerequisite fails, the permissive communication language does not authorize administration.
questions.stem: An adult presents a valid prescription with refills for an eligible long-acting injectable antipsychotic in single-dose packaging. The prescription lacks the suggested 'for pharmacist administration' notation. The trained pharmacist believes the prescriber intends pharmacy administration and has questions about the time since the last prescriber reassessment. Assume all other legal and clinical prerequisites are met. Which statements reflect DPH Circular DCP 26-03-124? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Contacting the prescriber to clarify the intended administration is encouraged in this situation.
choices.why: Correct. The circular encourages clarification when the notation is missing and pharmacy administration appears intended.

choices.text: Reject the prescription solely because the suggested administration notation is missing.
choices.why: Incorrect. The notation is recommended, not an independent mandatory validity element.

choices.text: Require a new prescription every quarter even if the current prescription has valid refills.
choices.why: Incorrect. Reassessment is at intervals determined by the prescriber and does not bar valid refills.

choices.text: Prescriber-determined reassessment intervals can coexist with a prescription that has valid refills.
choices.why: Correct. The circular explicitly distinguishes reassessment from refill validity.

choices.text: Treat a question about the reassessment interval as imposing mandatory prescriber contact in every case.
choices.why: Incorrect. Routine communication on such questions is encouraged, not required before administration in every case.

questions.citation: DPH Circular Letter DCP 26-03-124 (March 11, 2026), p. 3 Prescriber Assessment; pp. 4–5 Pharmacist-Prescriber Communication

questions.topic: Replacement paper prescription after electronic dispensing elsewhere
questions.trigger: A patient brings an otherwise lawful paper replacement for a Schedule IV prescription, under an applicable Massachusetts electronic-prescribing exception. The paper states that the prescription was originally sent electronically to Pharmacy A. Pharmacy B contacts Pharmacy A and learns that the electronic original was already dispensed. The paper represents the same order, not a new prescription. What should Pharmacy B do?
questions.legal_decision: Do not dispense the duplicate paper order and mark it void.
questions.critical_exception: Original electronic prescription already dispensed at another pharmacy; the later paper represents the same prescription.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If Pharmacy A had not dispensed the electronic original, it would have to void or cancel its electronic version before the paper replacement may be considered under other applicable rules.
questions.stem: A patient brings an otherwise lawful paper replacement for a Schedule IV prescription, under an applicable Massachusetts electronic-prescribing exception. The paper states that the prescription was originally sent electronically to Pharmacy A. Pharmacy B contacts Pharmacy A and learns that the electronic original was already dispensed. The paper represents the same order, not a new prescription. What should Pharmacy B do?

choices.text: Dispense the paper version because it is a different transmission format.
choices.why: Incorrect. A different format does not authorize dispensing the same controlled order twice.

choices.text: Do not dispense the paper version and mark that prescription void.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection (h) expressly requires both actions after confirming the original was dispensed.

choices.text: Ask Pharmacy A to void its completed dispensing record and then fill the replacement.
choices.why: Incorrect. A completed dispensing cannot be undone merely to permit a duplicate supply.

choices.text: Fill half the paper quantity without making any record of the prior dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Partial dispensing does not cure this duplicate-prescription prohibition.

choices.text: Treat the absence of the electronic record at Pharmacy B as proof the order was unfilled.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation requires checking with the other pharmacy.

questions.topic: Noncompliant EPCS application: immediate cessation and restart
questions.trigger: The vendor notifies a community pharmacy that its electronic controlled-substance prescription application no longer complies with DEA requirements. Pending an update, the manager wants to keep processing prescriptions through the same application because the screen still displays signatures. Which steps are required?
questions.legal_decision: Immediately cease controlled-substance prescription processing using that application; resume only after compliant-status notification and relevant updates.
questions.critical_exception: This is an identified noncompliant pharmacy application, not merely a printer outage or an unverified rumor.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the provider notifies the pharmacy that the application is again compliant and all relevant updates are installed, the specific application restriction is removed.
questions.stem: The vendor notifies a community pharmacy that its electronic controlled-substance prescription application no longer complies with DEA requirements. Pending an update, the manager wants to keep processing prescriptions through the same application because the screen still displays signatures. Which steps are required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Continue processing controlled prescriptions as long as the pharmacist recognizes the prescriber.
choices.why: Incorrect. The notification triggers immediate cessation using the noncompliant application.

choices.text: Resume as soon as an update is downloaded, even without compliant-status notification.
choices.why: Incorrect. Both the notification and installation of relevant updates are required.

choices.text: Immediately stop using the affected application to process controlled-substance prescriptions.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1311.200(c) explicitly requires this action.

choices.text: Treat vendor notification as applying only to Schedule II prescriptions.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule covers controlled-substance prescription processing generally.

choices.text: Resume only when notified that compliance is restored and all relevant updates are installed.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1311.200(d) provides both restart conditions.

questions.topic: Receiving electronic refill transfer: dispensing history
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a lawful electronic refill transfer of a Schedule IV prescription. The transferring pharmacy sends the original prescription data and remaining refill count, but omits the dates and locations of previous refills and the original dispensing pharmacy's identity, which differs from the transferring pharmacy. Which additional information is required for the receiving record?
questions.legal_decision: Obtain the missing previous-refill dates and locations, original dispensing pharmacy identifiers, and retain the receiving pharmacist's name with transferred information.
questions.critical_exception: This is an electronic transfer for refill purposes under 1306.25, not an initial unfilled EPCS transfer.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the transferring pharmacy was also the original filling pharmacy, the separate different-original-pharmacy information would not be required as an additional distinct set.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a lawful electronic refill transfer of a Schedule IV prescription. The transferring pharmacy sends the original prescription data and remaining refill count, but omits the dates and locations of previous refills and the original dispensing pharmacy's identity, which differs from the transferring pharmacy. Which additional information is required for the receiving record? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Obtain the dates and locations of previous refills.
choices.why: Correct. The electronic refill transfer must include this history.

choices.text: Replace the original dispensing date with the transfer date.
choices.why: Incorrect. The actual original dispensing date must be provided and preserved.

choices.text: Obtain the original filling pharmacy's name, address, DEA registration and prescription number because it differs.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection (b)(4)(v) requires this additional information when the original pharmacy differs.

choices.text: Create the electronic receiving record including the receiving pharmacist's name and transferred information.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection (b)(5) imposes this record duty on the recipient.

choices.text: Discard prior dispensing history once a new local prescription number is assigned.
choices.why: Incorrect. The new local identifier does not eliminate the required history.

questions.topic: Central-fill controlled-substance label identifies both pharmacies
questions.trigger: A properly authorized central-fill pharmacy prepares a Schedule II prescription for return to its participating retail pharmacy for final dispensing. The draft label includes all ordinary patient-specific federal information but identifies only the central-fill pharmacy by name and address. What correction does federal law require?
questions.legal_decision: Include the retail pharmacy name and address and the central-fill pharmacy's DEA registration number as the unique central-fill identifier.
questions.critical_exception: The prescription is centrally filled; all other applicable state and federal labeling requirements are assumed met.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the retail pharmacy filled the prescription itself, the special central-fill identifying requirement would not apply.
questions.stem: A properly authorized central-fill pharmacy prepares a Schedule II prescription for return to its participating retail pharmacy for final dispensing. The draft label includes all ordinary patient-specific federal information but identifies only the central-fill pharmacy by name and address. What correction does federal law require?

choices.text: Identify only the central-fill pharmacy because it physically prepared the package.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule additionally specifies the retail pharmacy identity and central-fill identifier.

choices.text: Identify only the retail pharmacy and omit the central-fill identifier.
choices.why: Incorrect. This omits the required information identifying central fulfillment.

choices.text: Use the retail pharmacy's DEA registration number as the only central-fill identifier.
choices.why: Incorrect. The unique identifier is the DEA number of the central-fill pharmacy.

choices.text: Show the retail pharmacy name and address and the central-fill pharmacy's DEA number.
choices.why: Correct. These are the specific additional central-fill label requirements.

choices.text: Replace all patient and prescription information with a barcode for the retail store.
choices.why: Incorrect. The ordinary required label information remains applicable.

questions.topic: OTC non-child-resistant single-size packaging
questions.trigger: A manufacturer supplies a household OTC drug that is subject to federal special packaging requirements. It offers compliant child-resistant packaging and proposes selling two different noncomplying package sizes for consumers with difficulty opening child-resistant closures. Which conditions apply to the manufacturer's noncomplying-packaging exception?
questions.legal_decision: Limit the noncomplying packaging to one size and require the conspicuous household warning on the required display panels, while supplying compliant packaging.
questions.critical_exception: This is the general retail manufacturer/packer exception, not a patient-request waiver for a dispensed prescription.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If only one noncomplying size is supplied with compliant packaging and the required conspicuous labeling, these particular packaging conditions are met.
questions.stem: A manufacturer supplies a household OTC drug that is subject to federal special packaging requirements. It offers compliant child-resistant packaging and proposes selling two different noncomplying package sizes for consumers with difficulty opening child-resistant closures. Which conditions apply to the manufacturer's noncomplying-packaging exception? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Offer only a single noncomplying package size under this exception.
choices.why: Correct. The manufacturer's noncomplying option is limited to a single size.

choices.text: Continue supplying the product in compliant special packaging.
choices.why: Correct. Availability of compliant packaging is an express condition.

choices.text: Use the patient waiver for each anonymous retail package in place of the retail rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. The individual prescription-packaging waiver is a different provision.

choices.text: Offer any number of noncomplying sizes if the drug is sold by a pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pharmacy retail sale does not expand the manufacturer's one-size exception.

choices.text: Place the required warning conspicuously on the relevant principal display panels.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation requires the warning on the immediate and applicable outer retail packaging, subject to the permitted alternate statement.

questions.topic: OTC tamper-evident packaging: two-piece hard gelatin capsules
questions.trigger: A retail pharmacist evaluates a publicly accessible OTC oral drug in two-piece hard gelatin capsules. It is subject to 21 CFR 211.132 and has no FDA exemption. The outer carton has an identifying tamper-evident feature, but the capsules are not sealed and the statement identifying the package feature would be destroyed when the carton is opened. Which packaging deficiencies should be identified?
questions.legal_decision: Require an acceptable tamper-evident capsule-sealing technology in addition to the required package feature; ensure the labeling statement identifies applicable features and remains unaffected if the feature is breached or missing.
questions.critical_exception: Covered two-piece hard gelatin capsule, publicly accessible at retail; no exemption.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the product were a covered tablet rather than a two-piece hard gelatin capsule, the additional capsule-sealing requirement would not apply, but the package and labeling requirements still would.
questions.stem: A retail pharmacist evaluates a publicly accessible OTC oral drug in two-piece hard gelatin capsules. It is subject to 21 CFR 211.132 and has no FDA exemption. The outer carton has an identifying tamper-evident feature, but the capsules are not sealed and the statement identifying the package feature would be destroyed when the carton is opened. Which packaging deficiencies should be identified? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The covered two-piece hard gelatin capsules require an acceptable tamper-evident sealing technology.
choices.why: Correct. Section 211.132(b)(2) adds capsule sealing to the package-feature requirement.

choices.text: The outer carton feature eliminates the separate requirement to seal these capsules.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule expressly requires the capsule seal in addition to the package feature.

choices.text: The required statement should identify applicable features and remain unaffected if they are breached.
choices.why: Correct. Section 211.132(c)(1) governs identification and placement of the statement.

choices.text: A child-resistant closure alone always substitutes for all tamper-evident packaging requirements.
choices.why: Incorrect. Tamper-evident and child-resistant packaging are separate regulatory requirements.

choices.text: The retail pharmacist can grant a manufacturer exemption from the capsule-sealing rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. An exemption is requested from FDA through the specified regulatory process.

questions.topic: MassPAT delegate leaves employment or loses authorization
questions.trigger: A pharmacy technician who has an approved MassPAT delegate sub-account leaves the pharmacy on a Monday. The primary account holder knows that the employee's delegated authorization has ended. Which actions are required under the MassPAT delegate rule?
questions.legal_decision: Inform DPH within one business day when authorization ends; retain responsibility for monitoring delegate use and compliance.
questions.critical_exception: The person is a delegate, not an independent primary account holder, and their authorization has ended.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the employee remains authorized and compliant, the departure-based notification trigger does not arise, while monitoring duties continue.
questions.stem: A pharmacy technician who has an approved MassPAT delegate sub-account leaves the pharmacy on a Monday. The primary account holder knows that the employee's delegated authorization has ended. Which actions are required under the MassPAT delegate rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Wait until the next annual pharmacy license renewal to notify DPH.
choices.why: Incorrect. The delegate authorization change has a one-business-day notice deadline.

choices.text: Inform the Department within one business day that the person is no longer an authorized delegate.
choices.why: Correct. Section 700.012(I)(3)(b) expressly imposes this deadline.

choices.text: Recognize that the primary account holder remains responsible for delegate use and monitoring.
choices.why: Correct. The primary holder has oversight and accountability duties.

choices.text: Allow the departing worker to use the same account until a replacement is hired.
choices.why: Incorrect. The ended authorization does not permit continued delegated access.

choices.text: Assume the delegate alone is responsible for every unauthorized query, with no responsibility for the primary holder.
choices.why: Incorrect. Subsection (I)(4) makes the primary account holder responsible for delegate use.

questions.topic: Cancellation of remaining items on an executed DEA Form 222
questions.trigger: A pharmacy sends an executed paper DEA Form 222 for multiple Schedule II products. Before the supplier ships one of the ordered items, the pharmacy determines that it no longer needs that item. The other items remain needed. Which steps comply with the federal cancellation rule?
questions.legal_decision: Notify the supplier in writing of partial cancellation; supplier marks canceled items on the original form by line-through and canceled notation.
questions.critical_exception: This is cancellation by the purchaser, not a defective order or expiration of the form.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the supplier instead initiates the voiding, it must notify the purchaser in writing and document the voiding in the prescribed manner.
questions.stem: A pharmacy sends an executed paper DEA Form 222 for multiple Schedule II products. Before the supplier ships one of the ordered items, the pharmacy determines that it no longer needs that item. The other items remain needed. Which steps comply with the federal cancellation rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Send the supplier written notice identifying the canceled item.
choices.why: Correct. The purchaser may cancel part or all of the order by written notification.

choices.text: Erase the unwanted item on the supplier's original form without further documentation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The supplier must preserve the prescribed cancellation notation.

choices.text: Cancel the entire order because partial cancellation is not permitted.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal rule expressly permits cancellation of part of the order.

choices.text: Have the supplier draw a line through the canceled item and print 'canceled' in the number-shipped space.
choices.why: Correct. This is the documentation prescribed for the original form.

choices.text: Require shipment and subsequent destruction because a signed Form 222 cannot be canceled.
choices.why: Incorrect. An executed order may be canceled under the stated process.

questions.topic: Unused DEA Forms 222 when pharmacy registration terminates
questions.trigger: A pharmacy permanently discontinues business and its DEA registration terminates. Several blank unused paper DEA Forms 222 remain in the secure office. The former owner proposes giving them to a neighboring pharmacy that has its own DEA registration. What is required?
questions.legal_decision: Return all unused Forms 222 to the DEA Registration Section rather than transferring them to another registrant.
questions.critical_exception: The purchaser's registration terminates; the forms are unused.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the registration remains active without a termination or specified suspension/revocation, this particular return trigger does not arise.
questions.stem: A pharmacy permanently discontinues business and its DEA registration terminates. Several blank unused paper DEA Forms 222 remain in the secure office. The former owner proposes giving them to a neighboring pharmacy that has its own DEA registration. What is required?

choices.text: Give the unused forms to another currently registered pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. The forms must be returned, not transferred between distinct registrants.

choices.text: Store them indefinitely with the purchaser's business records.
choices.why: Incorrect. Termination triggers return of unused forms.

choices.text: Use them to order inventory for the former owner's next pharmacy location.
choices.why: Incorrect. The terminated registration cannot support new orders.

choices.text: Destroy them as ordinary office paper without notifying DEA.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation expressly directs return of unused forms.

choices.text: Return all unused forms to the DEA Registration Section.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1305.18 states this duty on termination of registration.

questions.topic: DEA electronic prescription audit event: potential compromise
questions.trigger: The pharmacy's daily EPCS audit identifies an unauthorized modification attempt that could have compromised controlled prescription record integrity. The pharmacist confirms that it constitutes a security incident; the application is furnished by a service provider. No actual drug loss has yet been identified. Which steps are required under DEA's electronic prescription rules?
questions.legal_decision: Report the incident to DEA and applicable application service provider within one business day; retain the incident report.
questions.critical_exception: The incident compromised or could have compromised prescription-record integrity; no actual loss is required for this EPCS report.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the audit event is assessed and is not a security incident that compromised or could compromise integrity, this specific reporting requirement is not triggered.
questions.stem: The pharmacy's daily EPCS audit identifies an unauthorized modification attempt that could have compromised controlled prescription record integrity. The pharmacist confirms that it constitutes a security incident; the application is furnished by a service provider. No actual drug loss has yet been identified. Which steps are required under DEA's electronic prescription rules? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Wait for evidence of missing controlled inventory before reporting the EPCS incident.
choices.why: Incorrect. Potential compromise of prescription records triggers the rule independently of inventory loss.

choices.text: Report the qualifying incident to DEA within one business day.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1311.215(c) specifies the reporting deadline.

choices.text: Also notify the applicable pharmacy application service provider within one business day.
choices.why: Correct. The provider is an additional recipient when applicable.

choices.text: Allow the vendor to delete the incident record once the application is repaired.
choices.why: Incorrect. The registrant must retain a copy of the filed incident report.

choices.text: Retain a copy of the incident report in accordance with the applicable federal retention period.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1304.06 requires retention; the default federal period is two years.

questions.topic: Central fill of a Schedule IV refill: refill balance communication
questions.trigger: A participating Massachusetts retail pharmacy sends an otherwise lawful Schedule IV refill order to its authorized central-fill partner. It transmits the original prescription details but fails to include the previous refills dispensed and number remaining. Which step is required before processing the refill through this workflow?
questions.legal_decision: Transmit the number of refills already dispensed and number remaining in addition to required prescription information.
questions.critical_exception: Authorized central fill for a Schedule III-V prescription; distinct from transferring the prescription to another retail pharmacy.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the record already contains and transmits the accurate prior-refill and remaining-refill information, the stated data omission is resolved.
questions.stem: A participating Massachusetts retail pharmacy sends an otherwise lawful Schedule IV refill order to its authorized central-fill partner. It transmits the original prescription details but fails to include the previous refills dispensed and number remaining. Which step is required before processing the refill through this workflow?

choices.text: Allow the central-fill location to assume all originally authorized refills remain.
choices.why: Incorrect. This could cause dispensing beyond authorized refills and omits the required data.

choices.text: Send only the patient's name and current quantity, because central fill is not a retail transfer.
choices.why: Incorrect. Central fill has its own required prescription and refill information.

choices.text: Include the number of refills already dispensed and the number still remaining.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection (a)(3) expressly requires both values.

choices.text: Delete the original prescription after sending the refill order to the central-fill partner.
choices.why: Incorrect. The originating pharmacy must preserve the original for the required retention period.

choices.text: Use a new prescription number to restart the authorized refill balance.
choices.why: Incorrect. A new internal identifier does not change the prescriber's authorization.

questions.topic: DEA biennial inventory dictated rather than written
questions.trigger: During a biennial inventory, a pharmacist dictates complete controlled-substance counts into an audio recorder at closing time. The manager proposes retaining only the audio file indefinitely. Which actions satisfy the federal inventory-format rule?
questions.legal_decision: Promptly transcribe the dictated record into written, typewritten or printed form at the registered location and indicate the closing-business inventory time.
questions.critical_exception: An oral recording device may be used to take inventory, but the audio alone is not the required retained inventory form.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist originally produces a complete printed inventory at the registered location, no transcription of oral recordings is necessary.
questions.stem: During a biennial inventory, a pharmacist dictates complete controlled-substance counts into an audio recorder at closing time. The manager proposes retaining only the audio file indefinitely. Which actions satisfy the federal inventory-format rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Retain only the audio recording and omit a written or printed inventory.
choices.why: Incorrect. An inventory taken orally must be promptly transcribed.

choices.text: Promptly transcribe the audio into an appropriate written, typewritten or printed record.
choices.why: Correct. This is the specific condition for use of an oral recording device.

choices.text: Record a new inventory date based on when the transcription is finished.
choices.why: Incorrect. The inventory date is when the counts were taken.

choices.text: Omit the opening-versus-closing designation because the counts are complete.
choices.why: Incorrect. The record must specify whether it is as of opening or close of business.

choices.text: Indicate that the inventory was taken at close of business and maintain the required record at the registered location.
choices.why: Correct. Both are express requirements of subsection (a).

questions.topic: 503B intermediary wholesale distribution versus lawful administration
questions.trigger: A registered 503B outsourcing facility compounds a sterile drug. An unrelated distributor proposes purchasing the drug and reselling it as office stock to hospitals, while a hospital proposes obtaining it directly from the compounder and administering it to patients. Which conclusions reflect the federal 503B condition on sales and transfers?
questions.legal_decision: Do not route office-stock sales through a reseller as a qualifying 503B transfer; distinguish lawful administration and patient-specific dispensing from prohibited intermediary sales.
questions.critical_exception: Federal section 503B(a)(8) condition; assume other state and federal conditions for direct acquisition and use are met.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the hospital purchases directly from the actual compounding outsourcing facility and administers the drug in health care, the intermediary-resale concern is absent.
questions.stem: A registered 503B outsourcing facility compounds a sterile drug. An unrelated distributor proposes purchasing the drug and reselling it as office stock to hospitals, while a hospital proposes obtaining it directly from the compounder and administering it to patients. Which conclusions reflect the federal 503B condition on sales and transfers? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The proposed reseller arrangement conflicts with the 503B condition prohibiting sale or transfer by another entity.
choices.why: Correct. The statute generally requires the compounding outsourcing facility to be the selling or transferring entity.

choices.text: A distributor's ordinary wholesale license automatically removes the federal 503B condition.
choices.why: Incorrect. A wholesale license does not alter the statutory condition on compounded drugs.

choices.text: The statute does not prohibit administration of the compounded drug in a health care setting.
choices.why: Correct. Administration is expressly distinguished from the sales/transfer prohibition.

choices.text: The statute also does not prohibit lawful dispensing pursuant to a qualifying patient prescription.
choices.why: Correct. The statute expressly preserves dispensing under section 503(b)(1).

choices.text: The drug becomes FDA-approved merely because it is sold by a registered outsourcing facility.
choices.why: Incorrect. Registration and 503B exemption eligibility are not product approval.

questions.citation: 21 USC 353b(a)(8), (10); FDA draft wholesaling guidance (statute controls)

questions.topic: 503B office-use compounded drug label review
questions.trigger: A hospital receives a sterile compounded drug directly from its 503B outsourcing facility for use as office stock, without an identified-patient prescription. The drug label satisfies the other applicable statutory label requirements but omits the compounded-drug identification, office-use statement and not-for-resale statement. Which corrections are required by the federal 503B labeling condition?
questions.legal_decision: Require compounded-drug identification and both not-for-resale and office-use labeling for distribution without an identified-patient prescription.
questions.critical_exception: Office-stock distribution from a 503B facility, not ordinary 503A patient-specific dispensing.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If supplied pursuant to a prescription for an individual identified patient, the office-use-only statement is not triggered by that distribution, but the compounded-drug and not-for-resale statements remain.
questions.stem: A hospital receives a sterile compounded drug directly from its 503B outsourcing facility for use as office stock, without an identified-patient prescription. The drug label satisfies the other applicable statutory label requirements but omits the compounded-drug identification, office-use statement and not-for-resale statement. Which corrections are required by the federal 503B labeling condition? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Prominently identify the drug as compounded using the required or permitted comparable statement.
choices.why: Correct. Section 503B expressly requires identification as a compounded drug.

choices.text: Use a statement that the compound is FDA-approved because the facility is registered.
choices.why: Incorrect. Outsourcing registration does not establish FDA approval of the compounded product.

choices.text: Omit office-use identification whenever the purchaser is a licensed hospital.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute makes the office-use statement dependent on absence of an identified-patient prescription.

choices.text: Include the required not-for-resale statement.
choices.why: Correct. This statement is part of the statutory 503B labeling condition.

choices.text: Include the office-use-only statement for the described non-patient-specific distribution.
choices.why: Correct. The statutory condition expressly applies it in this situation.
